new_statements.quote: Vowels are pronounced either long or short. A long vowel is approximately twice as long in duration of pronunciation as a short vowel. Length is a significant feature, often being the minimal difference between two words, e.g., gumilit 'crowd each other' and gumilit 'strips rice grains' [macron on the second form lost in scanned]. Length, when it occurs, is on the second to the last vowel of a stem form, unless it is affected by affixation, e.g., muntalid 'sharpens a round point'. Length only occurs on vowels of open syllables. Vowels of closed syllables are always short.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Batad Ifugao has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so this is the first sourced statement: penultimate contrastive length on open syllables of the stem, with rightward shift under -an/-on suffixation. It does not contradict anything on record. Caveat for the site: Newell describes length, not stress; a penultimate-stress reading is an interpretation of the Philippine length/stress correlation, not his wording.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Newell never uses the word 'stress' or 'accent' anywhere in the sound-pattern sections (pp. 3-11) or the grammar sketch; the only prominence-like feature he describes is contrastive vowel length. When a stem has length it sits on the penultimate vowel of the stem, and only in an open syllable (closed-syllable vowels are always short). Whether a given stem carries length at all is lexical (gumilit vs gumīlit). This is the usual Philippine penultimate-length pattern that catalogs treat as penultimate stress, but the source itself frames it as a length feature, not stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Suffixation with -an or -on pulls the length one syllable rightward, onto the last syllable of the stem (talid + -an = talīdan); enclitic pronouns do not move it (muntālidda). A stem without surface length can show length on its final vowel when that syllable is opened by a following pronoun suffix (talin + -an + -na = talināna), which Newell explains as 'potential length' realised only in open syllables. Length is written with a macron (sec. 5.4, p. 7).
new_statements.identity_note: Newell 1993 describes specifically the Batad dialect of Ifugao spoken in the Batad valley of north-central Ifugao ('a few thousand' speakers; c. 50,000 for closely related dialects), and notes that other Ifugao dialects such as Bayninan and Gohang have a five-vowel system where Batad has six (sec. 5.3, p. 6). The Reid 1971 items opened were for Ilongot (rosettaproject_ilk_phon-1) and Amganad Ifugao (rosettaproject_ifa_phon-1), neither of which is Batad Ifugao.

sources.quote: The grammar sketch never uses the words 'stress' or 'accent' (a full-text search for stress/accent: zero hits). Its only prosodic statement: 'When verb stems of the cvcv pattern are inflected by suffixes -an or -on, the vowel length shifts to the second vowel.' This repeats the 1993 phonology sketch's length-shift-under-suffixation already recorded in the record's morphology_note; word prosody is treated as lexically specified vowel length, consistent with a lexical two-way contrast.
sources.note: Would let a reader verify that Newell's 1970 stress minimal pairs (gayang 'hawk'/'spear', qidew, qitulud) are entered in 1993 as length pairs, pinning the 1970-stress = 1993-length equivalence the record asserts; low priority because it cannot change the lexical coding.
